numpy: In NumPy, what is the shape of np.arange(3).reshape(3, 1) + np.arange(4)?
Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right: (3, 1) and (4,) become (3, 1) and (1, 4), and each size-1 dimension stretches, giving (3, 4).
What happens when you run np.ones(3) + np.ones(4) in NumPy?
It raises a broadcasting ValueError
It returns an array of shape (4,)
It returns an array of shape (3, 4)
It pads the shorter array with zeros
Trailing dimensions 3 and 4 are unequal and neither is 1, so the shapes cannot be broadcast together and NumPy raises a ValueError.
A NumPy array x has shape (2, 3) and v has shape (3,). What is the shape of x - v?
The (3,) array is treated as (1, 3) and broadcast across both rows, so the result keeps shape (2, 3). This is how you subtract a per-column mean.
In NumPy, a = np.arange(5); b = a[1:3]; b[0] = 99. What is a afterwards?
Basic slicing returns a view that shares memory with a, so writing b[0] changes a[1]. Use a[1:3].copy() if you need an independent array.
In NumPy, a = np.arange(5); c = a[[0, 2]]; c[0] = 99. What is a afterwards?
Indexing with a list of integers (fancy indexing) always returns a copy, so modifying c leaves a unchanged, unlike basic slicing which returns a view.
What does np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)[1, :] return?
array([4, 8])
Index 1 selects the second row of the 3 x 4 array, which holds the values 4 through 7. array([1, 5, 9]) would be column 1, selected with [:, 1].
For a = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4), what is the shape of a[:, 1]?
An integer index removes that dimension, so selecting column 1 gives a 1-D array of length 3. Use a[:, 1:2] or a[:, [1]] to keep shape (3, 1).
What does a[a % 2 == 0] return for a = np.arange(7)?
The condition builds a boolean mask, and indexing with a boolean mask returns a 1-D array of the elements where the mask is True.
Why is np.sqrt(arr) usually much faster than [math.sqrt(v) for v in arr] on a large NumPy array?
The loop runs in compiled code over a typed, contiguous buffer
NumPy caches the results of previous square roots in memory
NumPy automatically runs the operation on the GPU when one exists
Python list comprehensions are executed lazily, one item at a time
Vectorized ufuncs loop in C over raw typed memory, avoiding per-element Python object overhead. NumPy does not use the GPU on its own.
What does np.where(a > 2, a, 0) return for a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])?
array([2, 3])
array([3, 4])
With three arguments np.where picks elements from a where the condition is True and 0 elsewhere. With only the condition, it would return indices instead.
What does np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]).sum(axis=0) return?
array([4, 6])
array([3, 7])
array([10])
axis=0 collapses the rows, summing down each column: 1+3 and 2+4. axis=1 would sum across each row and give array([3, 7]).
For x with shape (3, 4), what is the shape of x.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)?
keepdims=True keeps the reduced axis with size 1, so the result is (3, 1) and broadcasts back against x, for example in x - x.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True).
What does np.array([[1, 5, 2], [7, 0, 3]]).argmax(axis=1) return?
array([1, 0])
array([5, 7])
array([3])
argmax returns positions, not values. In row 0 the maximum 5 is at index 1, and in row 1 the maximum 7 is at index 0.
What memory layout does np.zeros((3, 4)) use by default?
C order (row-major)
Fortran order (column-major)
Random order per call
Strided, non-contiguous
NumPy creates arrays in C order by default, so elements of each row are adjacent in memory. Pass order='F' for column-major layout.
a = np.zeros((3, 4)) is C-contiguous. What is true about a.T?
It is a view that is F-contiguous
It is a new C-contiguous copy
It is a view that is C-contiguous
It is a copy that is not contiguous
Transposing only swaps the strides without moving data, so a.T is a view, and the swapped strides make it Fortran-contiguous rather than C-contiguous.
What are the strides of np.arange(6, dtype=np.int64).reshape(2, 3)?
Strides are byte steps per axis. Each int64 is 8 bytes, and moving to the next row skips 3 elements, which is 24 bytes, so the strides are (24, 8).
A C extension requires a C-contiguous array, but your input is a transposed view. Which call gives it a valid array?
np.ascontiguousarray(x)
np.asanyarray(x)
np.asarray(x, order='K')
x.reshape(x.shape)
np.ascontiguousarray returns x unchanged if it is already C-contiguous and copies it into C order otherwise. asanyarray, asarray with order='K' and same-shape reshape keep the original layout.
For A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) and I = np.eye(2), how do A * I and A @ I differ?
A * I is elementwise and A @ I is a matrix product
Both compute the matrix product of A and I
A * I is a matrix product and A @ I is elementwise
Both are elementwise, but @ is faster
The * operator multiplies matching elements (giving a diagonal of 1 and 4), while @ performs matrix multiplication and returns A unchanged here.
You need x in A x = b for a square, well-conditioned matrix A. Which NumPy call is the recommended approach?
np.linalg.solve(A, b)
np.linalg.inv(A) @ b
np.linalg.det(A) * b
np.dot(A.T, b)
solve uses an LU factorization directly, which is faster and numerically more stable than forming the explicit inverse and multiplying.
What does np.linalg.det(np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])) return, up to floating-point rounding?
For a 2 x 2 matrix the determinant is ad - bc = 1*4 - 2*3 = -2. NumPy computes it through LU decomposition, so the printed value may be -2.0000000000000004.
pandas: In pandas, what is df.shape for a DataFrame with 3 rows and 2 columns?
shape returns a (rows, columns) tuple. df.size would return the total number of cells, 6.
In pandas, what is the type of df['price'] compared with df[['price']]?
A single column label returns a Series, while a list of labels, even with one item, returns a DataFrame.
Given s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=['x', 'y', 'z']), what does s['y'] return?
Square brackets with a label look up the index label, and 'y' maps to 20. To select by position, use s.iloc[1].
What does pd.Series([1, 2], index=['a', 'b']) + pd.Series([10, 20], index=['b', 'c']) produce?
pandas aligns on index labels before adding. Only 'b' exists in both, so it gets 2 + 10; labels present in one Series only become NaN.
A Series of mean scores indexed by team
A DataFrame with one row per original row
A single float: the overall mean score
A list of DataFrames, one per team
Grouping, selecting one column and aggregating gives one value per group, so the result is a Series whose index is the unique team values.
What kind of columns does df.groupby('k').agg({'v': ['sum', 'max']}) produce?
Two flat columns named sum and max, with no v level
A single column holding (sum, max) tuples
Flat columns named v_sum and v_max
Passing a list of functions per column creates a two-level column MultiIndex. Use named aggregation, such as agg(v_sum=('v', 'sum')), to get flat names.
You want a new column holding each row's group mean, with the same length as df. Which expression fits?
transform returns a result aligned to the original rows, so it can be assigned directly. agg and mean return one value per group, and expanding().mean() gives a running mean, not the group mean.
For df = pd.DataFrame({'k': ['a', 'a', 'b'], 'v': [1, None, 3]}), what is df.groupby('k')['v'].count() for group 'a'?
count excludes missing values, so only the 1 is counted. size counts rows regardless of NaN and would return 2 for group 'a'.
What join type does pd.merge(left, right, on='id') use when how is not given?
The default is how='inner', which keeps only keys present in both DataFrames. Rows with unmatched ids are dropped silently.
left has ids 1, 2, 3 and right has ids 1, 2, 4. How many rows does pd.merge(left, right, on='id', how='left') return, assuming unique ids?
A left join keeps every row of left. Id 3 has no match, so its right-side columns are filled with NaN, giving 3 rows.
Both DataFrames have a non-key column named x. What columns does pd.merge(l, r, on='id') produce?
Overlapping non-key columns get the default suffixes ('_x', '_y'). Pass suffixes=('_l', '_r') to choose different ones.
Which expression gives the number of missing values in each column of df?
isna() returns a boolean DataFrame and summing it counts the True values per column. count() returns non-missing values, and any() only says whether some exist.
What does df.dropna() do with its default arguments?
Drops rows that contain at least one NaN
Drops rows where every value is NaN
Drops columns that contain any NaN
The defaults are axis=0 and how='any'. Use how='all' to drop only fully empty rows, or axis=1 to drop columns.
pandas aggregations skip missing values by default (skipna=True), so the mean is (1 + 3) / 2. NumPy's np.mean on the raw array would return nan.
Given s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4], index=['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']), what are s.loc['a':'c'] and s.iloc[0:2]?
loc slices by label and includes the end label, while iloc slices by position and excludes the end, like a Python list.
Which statement reliably sets column b to 0 for rows where a > 5?
A single .loc call with a row mask and a column label writes into df. The chained version assigns into a temporary copy, which triggers a warning or does nothing.
df['ts'] holds datetime64 values. Which expression extracts the year of each timestamp?
Datetime properties of a Series are exposed through the .dt accessor. A plain Series has no year attribute, and .str is for string columns.
2024 is a leap year, so February has 29 days and adding one day lands on February 29. pandas handles calendar rules for you.
Which is the fastest way to double every value in a large numeric column df['a']?
np.multiply, like df['a'] * 2, is vectorized and runs in compiled code. apply and map call a Python function once per element, which is much slower.
What does df.apply(f, axis=1) pass to the function f?
Each cell value, one at a time
axis=1 applies the function across columns, so f receives one row at a time as a Series indexed by column names. The default axis=0 passes each column.
polars: In Polars, what do pl.read_csv('data.csv') and pl.scan_csv('data.csv') return?
A DataFrame and a LazyFrame
A LazyFrame and a DataFrame
Both return a DataFrame
Both return a LazyFrame
read_* functions load data eagerly into a DataFrame. scan_* functions only build a query plan as a LazyFrame, and nothing is read until you collect.
Which method executes a Polars LazyFrame query and returns a DataFrame?
.collect()
.run()
.compute()
.execute()
collect() runs the optimized query plan and materializes the result. compute() is the Dask equivalent, not a Polars method.
What is the main advantage of Polars lazy mode over eager mode?
A query optimizer can rewrite the whole plan before running it
Every operation is cached on disk between steps for reuse
It avoids having to choose column data types at all
It runs Python lambdas in parallel across all cores without the GIL
In lazy mode Polars sees the full query and applies optimizations such as predicate and projection pushdown before any data is processed.
In a Polars lazy query, what does predicate pushdown do with a .filter() placed after several other steps?
Applies the filter as early as possible, ideally during the scan
Moves the filter to the very end of the plan, after joins
Converts the filter into an inner join against the source
Runs the filter only on the first batch of rows read from the source
Pushing predicates toward the data source means fewer rows are read and processed by later steps, which saves both time and memory.
What does projection pushdown mean for pl.scan_parquet('big.parquet').select('a', 'b').collect()?
Only columns a and b are read from the file
All columns are read, then a and b are kept
The file is converted to CSV before reading
Only the first 1000 rows are read
The optimizer pushes the column selection into the scan, so the Parquet reader skips columns that the query never uses.
Which LazyFrame method prints the optimized query plan without running the query?
.explain()
.describe()
.schema_plan()
.show_graph_text()
explain() returns the plan as text after optimization, which is useful for checking that filters and projections were pushed down.
What in-memory data format is Polars built on?
Apache Arrow columnar format
Row-oriented Python dictionaries
NumPy object arrays per column
SQLite database pages in memory
Polars stores each column as Arrow-style contiguous buffers with a validity bitmap, which enables fast vectorized and cache-friendly processing.
Why can a Polars DataFrame often be converted to a PyArrow Table with df.to_arrow() very cheaply?
Both use the Arrow memory layout, so buffers can be shared
Polars compresses data before converting it
PyArrow reads the data back from a CSV file
Polars keeps a second, hidden copy of the data in Python lists
Because the memory layout matches, conversion can usually hand over existing buffers instead of copying every value.
What does pl.Series([1, None, 3]).null_count() return in Polars?
None
Polars represents missing values as null using a validity bitmap, and null_count() counts them. Note that float NaN is a separate value, not a null.
Which Polars call returns a DataFrame with a single column equal to column a times 2?
df.select(pl.col('a') * 2)
df.with_columns(pl.col('a') * 2)
df['a'].apply(lambda x: x * 2)
df.filter(pl.col('a') * 2)
select keeps only the expressions you pass. with_columns would return all existing columns, with a replaced by the doubled values.
How does df.with_columns(...) differ from df.select(...) in Polars?
with_columns keeps all existing columns and adds or replaces some
with_columns drops all columns that are not listed in it
select modifies the original DataFrame in place instead of returning a copy
select only works on LazyFrames, never on eager DataFrames
with_columns returns the original columns plus the new or overwritten ones, while select returns only the listed expressions. Neither modifies in place.
In Polars, how do you name the result of the expression pl.col('price') * 1.12 as price_with_tax?
(pl.col('price') * 1.12).alias('price_with_tax')
(pl.col('price') * 1.12).rename('price_with_tax')
(pl.col('price') * 1.12).name('price_with_tax')
(pl.col('price') * 1.12).as_('price_with_tax')
alias sets the output column name of an expression. Without it, the result keeps the name of the leftmost column, here price.
Which Polars expression returns 'adult' when age >= 18 and 'minor' otherwise?
pl.when(pl.col('age') >= 18).then(pl.lit('adult')).otherwise(pl.lit('minor'))
pl.if_(pl.col('age') >= 18).then(pl.lit('adult')).else_(pl.lit('minor'))
pl.col('age').where(pl.col('age') >= 18, 'adult', 'minor')
pl.case(pl.col('age') >= 18, pl.lit('adult'), pl.lit('minor'))
when / then / otherwise is the Polars conditional expression, and pl.lit marks plain strings as literal values rather than column names.
Which method of a Polars GroupBy object takes expressions to compute per group, as in df.group_by('team').____(pl.col('pts').sum())?
agg
transform
summarize
aggregate_by
group_by(...).agg(...) evaluates each expression within every group and returns one row per group.
What does df.with_columns(pl.col('x').sum().over('g').alias('g_total')) do in Polars?
Adds each row's group total of x, keeping all rows
Returns one row per group with the sum of x
Sorts the DataFrame by g, then by x
Computes a running cumulative sum of x
over() is a window function: it computes the aggregate per group and broadcasts it back to every row, like transform in pandas.
What is the purpose of Polars streaming execution?
Processing data in batches so it can exceed available RAM
Reading data from Kafka topics in real time
Sending query results to a web browser as they arrive
Running queries on multiple machines in a distributed cluster
The streaming engine runs a lazy query chunk by chunk instead of loading everything at once, so larger-than-memory datasets can be processed on one machine.
You want to filter a 200 GB Parquet dataset and write the result to disk without collecting it into memory. Which Polars API fits?
pl.scan_parquet(...).filter(...).sink_parquet('out.parquet')
pl.read_parquet(...).filter(...).write_parquet('out.parquet')
pl.read_parquet(...).lazy().filter(...).collect()
pl.DataFrame(...).filter(...).to_pandas().to_parquet('out.parquet')
sink_* methods run a LazyFrame with the streaming engine and write results directly to a file. read_parquet would load the full dataset into RAM first.
Why does df.with_columns(pl.col('x').map_elements(lambda v: v * 2)) run much slower than pl.col('x') * 2 in Polars?
It calls Python per value under the GIL, blocking native parallelism
map_elements always converts the whole DataFrame to pandas first
Lambdas force Polars to write temporary files to disk for each value
map_elements forces eager mode and disables the Arrow memory format
Native expressions run in multithreaded Rust code. A Python function must be called once per element while holding the GIL, so it is slow and single-threaded.
In Polars, why is df.with_columns(expr_a, expr_b, expr_c) generally preferred over three chained with_columns calls with one expression each?
Independent expressions in one context can run in parallel
Chained calls modify the DataFrame in place
Polars allows only one with_columns call per query
Chained calls convert data to row-oriented format
Polars evaluates the expressions inside a single select or with_columns concurrently on its thread pool, so grouping independent work together uses more cores.
A pandas user moves to Polars. Which pandas concept does a Polars DataFrame deliberately not have?
A row index
Column data types
Group-by aggregations
Joins between tables
Polars has no index: rows are identified by position or by ordinary columns. Operations that rely on index alignment in pandas use explicit join keys in Polars.
scipy: What is res.x, approximately, after res = scipy.optimize.minimize(lambda x: (x[0] - 3) ** 2, x0=[0])?
array([3.])
array([0.])
array([9.])
array([-3.])
minimize searches for the input that minimizes the function. (x - 3)^2 is smallest at x = 3, and the result is stored in res.x as an array.
In the OptimizeResult returned by scipy.optimize.minimize, which attribute holds the objective value at the solution?
res.fun
res.x
res.nit
res.jac
res.x is the solution point, res.fun the function value there, res.nit the iteration count and res.jac the gradient. Also check res.success.
You need the root of a continuous function f on [a, b] where f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs. Which SciPy function fits?
scipy.optimize.brentq
scipy.optimize.linprog
scipy.optimize.curve_fit
scipy.optimize.minimize_scalar
brentq is a robust bracketing root finder that requires a sign change on the interval. minimize_scalar finds minima, not roots.
What does popt, pcov = scipy.optimize.curve_fit(model, xdata, ydata) give you?
Fitted parameters and their estimated covariance
Predicted y values and residuals
The p-value and the correlation coefficient
The gradient and the Hessian of model
curve_fit runs nonlinear least squares. popt holds the best-fit parameters, and the square roots of the diagonal of pcov estimate their standard errors.
Which scipy.optimize.minimize method is a classic choice for a smooth problem with simple lower and upper bounds on each variable?
L-BFGS-B
BFGS
CG
Newton-CG
L-BFGS-B is a limited-memory quasi-Newton method that handles box bounds directly. Plain BFGS, CG and Newton-CG do not support bounds.
You must maximize profit 3x + 2y subject to linear inequality constraints. Which SciPy function is designed for this?
scipy.optimize.linprog
scipy.optimize.brentq
scipy.optimize.curve_fit
scipy.optimize.fsolve
linprog solves linear programs. It minimizes by convention, so you pass the negated objective, -3x - 2y, to maximize.
What is the defining property of scipy.interpolate.CubicSpline built from points (x, y)?
It passes through every point and has continuous second derivatives
It fits a single cubic polynomial to all points by least squares
It connects the points with straight line segments between knots
It smooths the data like a regression curve and may miss some points
A cubic spline is piecewise cubic, interpolates every data point exactly and is smooth up to the second derivative at the knots.
With f = scipy.interpolate.interp1d([0, 10], [0, 100]), what does f(2.5) return?
array(25.)
array(6.25)
array(2.5)
array(250.)
interp1d defaults to linear interpolation, and the line from (0, 0) to (10, 100) has slope 10, giving 25 at x = 2.5.
Why use scipy.signal.filtfilt instead of scipy.signal.lfilter with the same filter coefficients?
It filters forward and backward, giving zero phase shift
It runs the same filter on the GPU for faster results
It designs the filter coefficients for you automatically
It works only on complex-valued signals such as I/Q data
filtfilt applies the filter twice in opposite directions, cancelling the phase delay. lfilter is causal and shifts features in time.
What does peaks, _ = scipy.signal.find_peaks(x) return in peaks?
Indices of the local maxima in x
Values of the local maxima in x
Frequencies of the strongest components
A boolean mask the same length as x
find_peaks returns the sample indices of peaks, plus a dictionary of properties. Use x[peaks] to get the peak heights.
A signal is sampled at fs = 1000 Hz. Which low-pass cutoff is invalid for scipy.signal.butter(4, cutoff, fs=1000)?
600 Hz
50 Hz
200 Hz
450 Hz
The cutoff must be below the Nyquist frequency, fs / 2 = 500 Hz. SciPy raises a ValueError for 600 Hz.
Which scipy.signal function estimates the power spectral density of a noisy signal by averaging overlapping segments?
welch
butter
convolve
find_peaks
Welch's method splits the signal into overlapping windowed segments and averages their periodograms, reducing variance compared with a single FFT.
What does scipy.stats.norm.cdf(0) return?
The standard normal is symmetric around 0, so half its probability lies below 0. 0.3989 is the density at 0, norm.pdf(0).
What does scipy.stats.norm.ppf(0.975) return, approximately?
ppf is the inverse of the CDF. The value with 97.5% of the standard normal below it is about 1.96, the familiar bound of a 95% two-sided interval.
For d = scipy.stats.norm(loc=10, scale=2), what are d.mean() and d.std()?
For the normal distribution, loc is the mean and scale is the standard deviation, not the variance. The variance here is 4.
You compare exam scores of two separate groups of students. Which scipy.stats function performs the standard t-test?
ttest_ind
ttest_rel
ttest_1samp
pearsonr
ttest_ind tests two independent samples. ttest_rel is for paired measurements on the same subjects, and ttest_1samp compares one sample with a constant.
Which method gives the probability that a scipy.stats.poisson(mu=3) variable equals exactly 2?
poisson.pmf(2, mu=3)
poisson.pdf(2, mu=3)
poisson.cdf(2, mu=3)
poisson.ppf(2, mu=3)
Discrete distributions expose pmf for point probabilities. Continuous distributions use pdf instead, and cdf would give P(X <= 2).
Why store a large matrix with 0.1% nonzero entries in scipy.sparse?
Only nonzero values and their positions are stored
Sparse formats compress values with lossy rounding
Sparse matrices are automatically moved to the GPU
Dense NumPy arrays cannot hold that many zeros
Sparse formats such as CSR keep only nonzeros plus index arrays, cutting memory and letting operations skip zero entries.
Which scipy.sparse format is best for fast matrix-vector products and row slicing?
CSR
COO
LIL
DOK
Compressed Sparse Row stores rows contiguously, which suits row access and products. COO, LIL and DOK are convenient for building a matrix, then you convert to CSR.
Which call converts a scipy.sparse matrix or array A to a dense NumPy array?
A.toarray()
A.densify()
np.sparse(A)
A.to_numpy()
toarray() returns a dense ndarray. Be careful on large matrices, since the dense version stores every zero explicitly.
matplotlib: What does fig, ax = plt.subplots() return in Matplotlib?
A Figure and a single Axes
An Axes and a list of Figures
Two Axes objects in a tuple
A Figure and a NumPy array of Axes
With no grid arguments, plt.subplots creates one Figure containing one Axes and returns both. A grid such as (2, 2) returns an array of Axes instead.
In Matplotlib, what is an Axes object?
One plot area with its own coordinate system, inside a Figure
The whole window or image that holds every plot and figure
A single x or y axis line, together with its tick marks and labels
A saved image file on disk that contains the plot
A Figure is the top-level container, and each Axes is a plotting region with x and y Axis objects, a title and labels.
Which call sets the x-axis label on an Axes object ax?
ax.set_xlabel('Time (s)')
ax.xlabel('Time (s)')
ax.label_x('Time (s)')
ax.xaxis_label('Time (s)')
The object-oriented API uses set_ prefixed methods such as set_xlabel and set_title. plt.xlabel exists only in the pyplot state-based interface.
What is axes.shape after fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3)?
A grid with more than one row and column returns a 2-D NumPy array of Axes, indexed as axes[row, col].
What is axes.shape after fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3)?
With the default squeeze=True, a single row or column is returned as a 1-D array. Pass squeeze=False to always get a 2-D array.
You plot four related time series in a 2 x 2 grid and want zooming in one to zoom all of them along x. Which option fits?
plt.subplots(2, 2, sharex=True)
plt.subplots(2, 2, linkx=True)
plt.subplots(2, 2, sync='x')
plt.subplots(2, 2, samex=True)
sharex=True makes all subplots share one x-axis, so limits and zoom stay in sync. sharey does the same for the y-axis.
Axis labels in your subplot grid overlap neighboring plots. Which fix is the standard one?
Call fig.tight_layout() or use layout='constrained'
Increase plt.rcParams['font.size'] for all text
Call ax.autoscale() on every Axes in the grid
Save the figure with dpi=300 so the text renders more sharply
Both tight_layout and the constrained layout engine adjust subplot spacing to fit labels and titles. Higher dpi or font size makes overlap worse, not better.
Which call applies the built-in ggplot style to all plots created afterwards in a script?
plt.style.use('ggplot')
plt.theme('ggplot')
plt.set_style('ggplot')
plt.rc('style', 'ggplot')
plt.style.use loads a style sheet into rcParams globally. plt.style.available lists the names of the built-in styles.
What does plt.rcParams['font.size'] = 14 do?
Changes the default font size for later plot elements
Resizes text only in the current Axes
Updates fonts in figures already saved to disk
Sets the font size of the title only
rcParams holds global defaults. Text created after the change uses the new size, while existing artists and saved files are not modified.
In ax.scatter(x, y, s=50), what does s control?
Marker size, as an area in points squared
Marker size, as a radius in pixels
The shade of the marker color
Spacing between neighboring markers
s is the marker area in points^2, so doubling the visible width of a marker requires about four times the s value.
What is the default colormap for ax.imshow and ax.scatter color values in Matplotlib 2.0 and later?
viridis
jet
rainbow
gray
Matplotlib 2.0 replaced jet with viridis as the default because viridis is perceptually uniform and readable in grayscale and for many color-blind viewers.
You map temperature anomalies that range from -3 to +3 degrees, centered on zero. Which kind of colormap fits best?
A diverging map such as 'RdBu'
A sequential map such as 'Blues'
A qualitative map such as 'tab10'
A cyclic map such as 'twilight'
Diverging colormaps use a neutral middle color with two contrasting hues, which highlights deviations above and below a meaningful center.
How do you get the reversed version of the viridis colormap by name?
cmap='viridis_r'
cmap='-viridis'
cmap='reverse_viridis'
cmap='rev_viridis'
Every registered colormap has a reversed twin named with an _r suffix. A Colormap object also offers a .reversed() method.
Which call adds a color scale bar for the image returned by im = ax.imshow(data)?
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax)
ax.colorbar(im)
im.add_colorbar(ax)
plt.legend(handles=[im])
colorbar needs the mappable (here the AxesImage) to know the colormap and normalization. A legend is for labeled lines and markers, not color scales.
How many bins does ax.hist(data) use when bins is not specified, with default rcParams?
'auto'
The default comes from rcParams['hist.bins'], which is 10. Pass bins='auto' or an integer for a better choice on your data.
You need to show how many students chose each of five programming languages. Which chart is the right choice?
A bar chart with ax.bar
A histogram with ax.hist
A line chart with ax.plot
A scatter plot with ax.scatter
Bar charts compare counts across categories. Histograms bin continuous numeric values, and a line chart implies an order between the languages.
You call plt.savefig('chart.svg'). What kind of file is produced?
A vector SVG, with the format inferred from the extension
A PNG raster image that is simply renamed to .svg
A raster image at 300 dpi saved with an .svg name
An error, since the format argument must always be passed explicitly
savefig infers the format from the file extension. SVG, PDF and EPS are vector formats that stay sharp at any zoom level.
Your saved chart has large empty margins. Which savefig option trims them?
bbox_inches='tight'
margins='none'
crop='tight'
trim_margins=True
bbox_inches='tight' computes the tight bounding box of the drawn content and crops the output to it. pad_inches controls the remaining padding.
You want text in SVG exports to stay as real, editable text instead of being converted to paths. Which setting does this?
plt.rcParams['svg.fonttype'] = 'none'
plt.rcParams['svg.fonttype'] = 'path'
plt.rcParams['text.usetex'] = True
plt.rcParams['svg.text'] = 'editable'
The default 'path' converts glyphs to outlines. 'none' writes text elements and relies on the viewer having the font installed.
In a script you call plt.show() and then plt.savefig('out.png'), and the saved file is blank. What is the fix?
Call plt.savefig before plt.show
Pass transparent=False to savefig
Use a .jpg extension instead of .png
Call plt.clf() before savefig
In a non-interactive script, closing the window shown by plt.show() releases the figure, so the later savefig writes a new empty figure. Saving first avoids this.
opencv: In what channel order does cv2.imread return a color image?
BGR
RGB
RGBA
HSV
OpenCV stores color images as blue, green, red by default for historical reasons. Libraries such as Matplotlib expect RGB.
Colors look wrong when you display a cv2.imread image with plt.imshow. Which call fixes it?
cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)
cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
cv2.normalize(img, None, 0, 255)
img.astype('float32') / 255
Converting BGR to RGB swaps the red and blue channels so Matplotlib shows true colors. Normalizing or changing the dtype does not reorder channels.
A color photo is 640 pixels wide and 480 pixels high. What is img.shape after cv2.imread?
OpenCV images are NumPy arrays in (rows, columns, channels) order, so height comes first, then width, then the three color channels.
What does cv2.imread('missing.jpg') do if the file does not exist?
It returns None silently
It raises FileNotFoundError
It returns an empty black image
It raises a cv2.error
imread does not raise on a missing or unreadable file, it returns None. Check for None before use, or later calls fail with confusing errors.
How do you read the pixel at horizontal position x and vertical position y of a NumPy image img?
img[y, x]
img[x, y]
img.at(x, y)
img[x][y][0]
Arrays are indexed by row first, and the row is the vertical coordinate. Mixing up x and y is a common source of bugs.
You want an output image 320 pixels wide and 240 pixels high. Which call is correct?
cv2.resize(img, (320, 240))
cv2.resize(img, (240, 320))
cv2.resize(img, 320, 240, 3)
cv2.resize(img, shape=(240, 320))
The dsize argument of cv2.resize is (width, height), which is the reverse of the NumPy shape order (height, width).
Which pair of calls rotates an image by 30 degrees around its center?
cv2.getRotationMatrix2D, then cv2.warpAffine
cv2.getPerspectiveTransform, then cv2.warpAffine
cv2.rotate with an angle of 30
cv2.findHomography, then cv2.remap
getRotationMatrix2D builds a 2 x 3 affine matrix from a center, angle and scale, and warpAffine applies it. cv2.rotate only supports 90 degree steps.
How many point correspondences do cv2.getAffineTransform and cv2.getPerspectiveTransform require?
3 and 4
4 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 3
An affine transform has 6 unknowns, fixed by 3 point pairs. A perspective transform (homography) has 8, so it needs 4 pairs.
Which property does an affine transform preserve that a general perspective transform does not?
Parallel lines remain parallel
Straight lines remain straight
The image size in pixels stays fixed
The color channels remain ordered
Both transforms map straight lines to straight lines, but only affine maps keep parallel lines parallel. Perspective makes them converge.
For an 8-bit image converted with cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV, what is the range of the hue channel?
Hue in degrees (0 to 359) does not fit in 8 bits, so OpenCV halves it to 0 to 179. Saturation and value use 0 to 255.
What does cv2.inRange(hsv, lower, upper) return?
A single-channel mask, 255 where pixels are in range
The pixels in range, with others set to black
The count of pixels inside the range
A list of contours inside the range
inRange produces a binary mask. Combine it with cv2.bitwise_and(img, img, mask=mask) to keep only the matching colors.
What does cv2.threshold(gray, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY) return?
A tuple of the threshold value used and the output image
Only the thresholded image as a NumPy array
A boolean NumPy array marking pixels above 127
A list of pixel coordinates above the threshold value 127
threshold returns (retval, dst). With a fixed threshold, retval is 127; with Otsu it is the computed value. Forgetting to unpack is a common bug.
What does adding cv2.THRESH_OTSU to cv2.THRESH_BINARY in cv2.threshold do?
Computes the threshold from the histogram and ignores the given value
Applies the threshold separately to each color channel of the image
Inverts the output so that the objects become black on white
Uses a different threshold for each image region based on its neighbors
Otsu's method picks the threshold that best separates the two histogram classes, which works well for bimodal images. It requires a single-channel grayscale image.
A scanned document has strong shadows on one side, so a single global threshold fails. Which function fits?
cv2.adaptiveThreshold
cv2.equalizeHist
cv2.fastNlMeansDenoising
cv2.morphologyEx
adaptiveThreshold computes a separate threshold for each pixel from its neighborhood, handling uneven lighting that defeats one global value.
In cv2.Canny(img, 50, 150), what happens to a pixel whose gradient magnitude is 100?
It is kept only if connected to a strong edge
It is always kept as an edge pixel in the output
It is always discarded as weak edge noise
It is always kept, since it is above the lower threshold
Canny uses hysteresis: above 150 is a strong edge, below 50 is rejected, and values between are kept only when they connect to a strong edge.
In OpenCV 4.x, what does cv2.findContours(binary, cv2.RETR_TREE, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE) return?
contours and hierarchy
image, contours and hierarchy
Only a list of contours
A labeled image of regions
OpenCV 4.x returns two values. OpenCV 3.x returned three, with the image first, which is why old tutorials unpack three values.
findContours returns one huge contour around the whole image instead of around your dark objects on a white background. What is the likely fix?
Invert the binary image so the objects are white
Convert the image from BGR to RGB before thresholding
Use cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_NONE instead of SIMPLE
Increase the image resolution before the call
findContours treats nonzero (white) pixels as foreground. Use THRESH_BINARY_INV or cv2.bitwise_not so the objects are white on black.
You need only the outer boundary of each object, ignoring holes inside them. Which retrieval mode fits cv2.findContours?
cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL
cv2.RETR_TREE
cv2.RETR_FLOODFILL
cv2.RETR_CCOMP
RETR_EXTERNAL returns only the outermost contours. RETR_TREE and RETR_CCOMP also return inner contours and a hierarchy, and RETR_FLOODFILL is a special mode meant for flood-fill segmentation.
An image has salt-and-pepper noise (random white and black pixels). Which filter removes it best?
cv2.medianBlur
cv2.blur
cv2.Sobel
cv2.filter2D
A median filter replaces each pixel with the neighborhood median, so isolated outliers disappear. A box blur only spreads them out.
You want to smooth skin texture in a portrait but keep sharp edges around the face. Which filter is designed for this?
cv2.bilateralFilter
cv2.GaussianBlur
cv2.blur
cv2.Laplacian
A bilateral filter weights neighbors by both distance and intensity difference, so it smooths flat regions without averaging across strong edges.
